newsitem.title: UK: Indian finance minister sticks to economic targets.
newsitem.headline: Indian finance minister sticks to economic targets.

text.p: Despite mounting evidence to the contrary, India's Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram is adhering to his ambitious growth target of 6.5 percent for the Indian economy in fiscal 1996/97.
"I have no reason to believe we will achieve less than 6.5 percent after 6.5-7.0 percent last year," he told a news conference in London on Thursday.
Economists believe that India may be hard-pushed to achieve more than 5.5 percent this year as key sectors of the economy are growing more slowly than last.

Production of crude oil, steel, oil products, cement and coal grew at just 3.5 percent in April to August this year compared with 11.7 percent in the same 1995 period, but Chidambaram disputed this was a problem as other areas were outperforming.
"Last year, the agricultural sector grew very slowly, just 2.1 percent, this year the monsoon was very good and indications are we will have a record year in agriculture," he said.
Chidamabaram, who was in London on his way to the International Monetary Fund meeting in Washington does not believe that criticism of India's burgeoning budget deficit is justified.
"I believe that we can cut the deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in my term of office, I have five years, but I would like to achieve it in four," he said.
The government estimates that the fiscal deficit as a share of the GDP will fall to 5.0 percent in 1996/97 from 5.9 percent in 1995/96.
Last year, the IMF called for bolder steps in order to cut the deficit and some of Chidambaram's new spending commitments have raised questions over his ability to achieve this.

Despite his ambitious budget targets, the finance minister said that the three month and twenty five day-old United Front-Left Front government, a coalition of 14 parties including communists, remains committed to welfare.
"The main difference between this government and the last are on concerns of social justice," he said.

However, analysts note that the effect of this is to empower regions and boost aid to farmers and the poor, while new taxes such as the minimum corporate tax of 12.9 percent will do little to plug the gaps in the budget.

Chidambaram said that the new government remained committed to speeding approvals of foreign investment, it is targetting $10 billion a year compared with just $2.0 billion in 1995/96, as part of its programme to lift growth and quadruple household income over the next 25 years.
"Reforms are continiung and the new government is determined to take those reforms forward," he said.
